title: Why Our BDD Failed
subtitle: Six hundred scenarios, three hours a night, nobody reads them. Is Cucumber really the problem?

briefing.heading: Case briefing
paragraphs: **Lumen Insurance** is a fictional insurer. Eighteen months ago its Quotes team adopted Cucumber-JVM with JUnit 5 for the platform that prices car and home policies. The plan sounded simple: write the tests in plain-language Gherkin so everyone could read them.

Today the Quotes suite has 600 scenarios. The nightly run takes three hours and is red most mornings. The product owner has stopped opening the feature files. At the last planning meeting the head of engineering proposed dropping Cucumber altogether and rewriting everything as plain JUnit tests.
Before that decision is made, you've been asked to find out what actually went wrong. Everyone has a theory. The evidence is in the repo, the pipeline, the calendar and the people.
briefing.question: Why did Lumen's Cucumber suite become slow, brittle and unread?
briefing.stakes: Search the locations, pin what you find, rule theories out with evidence, then name the cause.

detective.title: You are the new engineering manager for Lumen's Quotes platform
detective.description: You know Java and testing. You don't need to be a Cucumber expert; you need to read the evidence and ask what each clue can and cannot prove.

cast.name: Marcus Bell
cast.bio: Wants to drop Cucumber. Has watched the nightly build go red for a year.

cast.name: Victor Hale
cast.bio: Signed off the Cucumber adoption plan. Measures success in automated scenarios.

cast.name: Tom Reyes
cast.bio: Thinks the whole stack is too heavy. Keeps a cucumber-js prototype on a branch.

cast.name: Lena Park
cast.bio: Runs the CI pool. Owns the nightly Quotes job and its retry settings.

cast.name: Iris Mensah
cast.bio: Writes the story tickets. Stopped reading the feature files months ago.

cast.name: Dana Okafor
cast.bio: Her team wrote nearly every scenario in the suite.

cast.name: Sam Lindqvist
cast.bio: Runs a Cucumber suite in the same company that finishes in six minutes.

hypotheses.title: Cucumber is slow and flaky
hypotheses.statement: Cucumber and Gherkin add a slow, flaky layer on top of our tests. Drop it and write plain JUnit tests instead.
hypotheses.tempting: The suite really is slow and flaky, and Cucumber's name is on every failure in the log. When a tool is always present at the scene, it's natural to suspect it.
hypotheses.why: The Claims team runs the same Cucumber-JVM, in the same company, in six minutes and green almost every night, and the lab shows Quotes scenarios getting fast once they're rewritten and run below the UI. The slowness comes from how the scenarios are written and wired, not from the tool.

hypotheses.title: The testers aren't skilled enough
hypotheses.statement: The QA team wrote poor scenarios. With stronger automation engineers the suite would be fine.
hypotheses.tempting: Testers wrote nearly every scenario, so poor scenarios look like poor testers.
hypotheses.why: Their automation code is competent, and they followed the adoption plan exactly: convert manual test cases into feature files after each release. The plan left out the conversations that make BDD work, and no amount of skill could put them back in.

hypotheses.title: Java was the wrong choice
hypotheses.statement: Java makes everything heavy. We should have used JavaScript and cucumber-js.
hypotheses.tempting: Java projects can feel verbose, and switching stacks always feels like a fresh start.
hypotheses.why: Claims uses Java too and is fast. In Quotes, 90% of the run time is spent driving the browser, which any language would do at the same speed.

hypotheses.title: The CI servers are underpowered
hypotheses.statement: Our CI machines are too small for 600 scenarios. Bigger machines would fix the run time.
hypotheses.tempting: Slow builds and an old CI pool make hardware the obvious suspect, and asking for more is easy.
hypotheses.why: The CI node sits at 9% CPU because parallel execution is switched off, and the Claims suite runs on the same servers in six minutes. More hardware can't speed up a suite that runs one scenario at a time.

hypotheses.title: BDD was adopted as test automation only
hypotheses.statement: We bought the tool and skipped the practice. Nobody discussed examples before building, so testers turned old test cases into UI click scripts after each release. Those scripts share state, can't run in parallel and need retries to pass.
hypotheses.why: Every clue points at how Cucumber was used. Gherkin was written weeks after the code, by QA alone, from manual test cases (the memo, the commit history, the story flow). The steps are imperative click scripts the product owner can't read. Shared logins and static fields forced parallel runs off, a 120-row Outline and a 46-step journey bloat the run, 90% of the time is spent in the browser, and retries hide the flakiness. The same tool, used as a collaboration practice, runs in six minutes next door.

clues.title: Scenarios are click scripts
clues.text: A Quotes feature file reads: When I click "#get-quote" / And I wait 3 seconds / And I type "34" into "input[name=age]" / Then ".premium" shows "£412".
clues.proves: The scenarios describe UI mechanics (selectors, waits, clicks), not business behaviour.
clues.why: Imperative steps break whenever the screen changes and say nothing a product owner can check. Cucumber's own guidance prefers declarative steps that describe what the system does, leaving the how to the step definitions.

clues.title: One login for everything
clues.text: The test-data sheet: every scenario logs in as qa_user_1. A note in red: "Renewal scenarios fail unless run in file order."
clues.proves: Scenarios share data and depend on the order they run in.
clues.why: Cucumber's docs say scenarios must be independent and must not share state. Shared accounts force a slow, fragile, one-at-a-time run.

clues.title: Request for 64-core machines
clues.text: A printed ticket: "Request: 64-core CI machines so the Cucumber suite can finish overnight."
clues.proves: Someone believes hardware is the bottleneck.
clues.why: It's a natural request when builds are slow, but a request is a belief, not evidence of the cause.

clues.title: Plan: QA converts tests later
clues.text: The adoption memo: "QA will convert existing manual test cases into feature files after each release. Developers and product are not expected to change how they work."
clues.proves: BDD was adopted purely as test automation, done by QA after development.
clues.why: BDD's value starts with a conversation before code: discovery, then formulation in Gherkin, then automation. Writing Gherkin after release skips the first two and turns scenarios into expensive regression scripts.

rulesOut.because: The testers did exactly what the plan asked. It was the plan, not their skill, that left them working alone at the end of the process.

clues.title: Parallel off, retries on
clues.text: quotes-nightly.yml: cucumber.execution.parallel.enabled=false, and failed scenarios are retried up to twice.
clues.proves: The suite runs one scenario at a time, and flaky failures are rerun until they pass.
clues.why: Parallel was switched off because scenarios share state. Retries make a red build go green without fixing anything.

rulesOut.because: With parallel execution switched off, bigger servers would sit just as idle: the run is limited to one scenario at a time by its own configuration.

clues.title: Java 17 to 21 last month
clues.text: The pipeline moved from Java 17 to Java 21 last month.
clues.proves: There was a recent change to the build.
clues.why: Recent changes always look suspicious, but the run history shows the suite was slow and red for over a year before it.

clues.title: 90% of the time in the browser
clues.text: Last night's report: 2 h 46 min of the 3 h 04 min run was spent in browser-driven steps.
clues.proves: Almost all the run time goes into driving the UI.
clues.why: Declarative scenarios can be automated below the UI, against the API, for most business rules. That's where most of a suite's speed comes from.

rulesOut.because: The time is spent in the browser, not in Java. Step definitions in another language would drive the same browser just as slowly.

clues.title: One Outline, 120 rows
clues.text: premium_by_age_and_region.feature: one Scenario Outline with 120 Examples rows, each driven through the UI. 22 minutes on its own.
clues.proves: Every combination was put into Gherkin instead of a few telling examples.
clues.why: BDD examples illustrate rules for people: a few cases at the boundaries. The full matrix belongs in fast unit tests.

clues.title: 41 passed only on retry
clues.text: Last night 37 scenarios failed and 41 more passed only on a retry. Nine of them have needed a retry every night for a month.
clues.proves: Flakiness is widespread, and retries are hiding it.
clues.why: Small per-scenario flakiness multiplies across hundreds of scenarios. Retries mask it, and they mask real intermittent bugs along with it.

clues.title: Feature files weeks after code
clues.text: Commit history: Quotes feature files are added five to six weeks after the code merges, always by the QA team. Claims adds theirs before the code.
clues.proves: Gherkin is written after the behaviour is built, by one team alone.
clues.why: Scenarios written after the fact can't shape what gets built. They only record it, usually in the language of the screen.

clues.title: No conversation before building
clues.text: The story flow: ticket, build, release, then QA writes the feature file. At no point do product, development and testing discuss examples together.
clues.proves: The discovery part of BDD never happens.
clues.why: Discovery sessions such as Example Mapping (yellow story, blue rules, green examples, red questions) are where a team agrees on behaviour before code. Without them, Cucumber is only a test runner with extra steps.

clues.title: Same tool, six minutes
clues.text: Claims team: same Cucumber-JVM 8, Java, JUnit 5 and CI servers. 140 declarative scenarios, 8 parallel workers, six minutes, green 99% of nights.
clues.proves: The tool, the language and the servers can all produce a fast, reliable suite.
clues.why: When the same tool behaves completely differently in two teams, the difference is how it's being used.

rulesOut.because: Cucumber runs fast and green for the Claims team in the same company, so the tool itself isn't the cause.
Claims writes its step definitions in Java too, and its suite is fast.
Claims runs on the same CI servers and finishes in six minutes.

clues.title: Static fields in step classes
clues.text: QuoteSteps.java opens with: private static WebDriver driver; private static Policy currentPolicy; and every step class reads and writes them.
clues.proves: State leaks from one scenario to the next through static fields.
clues.why: Cucumber-JVM creates fresh step-definition instances for every scenario. Statics defeat that. A per-scenario context object injected with PicoContainer keeps scenarios independent, which is what allows parallel runs.

clues.title: Rewritten and rewired: six minutes
clues.text: In Sam's trial, a slice of Quotes scenarios rewritten declaratively, wired to the API and given their own data runs at a pace that would finish the whole suite in about six minutes.
clues.proves: The same tool gets fast once scenarios are independent and run below the UI.
clues.why: Speed comes from how scenarios are written and automated, which is a team practice, not a tool setting.

rulesOut.because: With the same Cucumber, the run drops from hours to minutes once the scenarios change. The tool was never the bottleneck.

clues.title: The product owner can't read them
clues.text: Iris: "They're all clicks, selectors and waits. I can't tell which business rule any of them checks."
clues.proves: The feature files no longer work as shared documentation.
clues.why: Gherkin's point is a specification the business can read and correct. If the product owner can't, the scenarios have become test code in disguise.

clues.title: CI servers 9% busy
clues.text: During the three-hour run, the CI node averages 9% CPU, with only one core busy.
clues.proves: The servers are mostly idle while the suite runs.
clues.why: A suite that has to run one scenario at a time can't use more hardware, however much you buy.

rulesOut.because: Underpowered servers would be maxed out during the run; these idle at 9%.

clues.title: The testers are strong engineers
clues.text: Dana: two of her testers are certified in browser automation and built a clean page-object framework; code reviews rate their Java highly.
clues.why: Skilled automation of the wrong thing, at the wrong time, still gives a poor suite. BDD is a team practice before it is a coding task.

rulesOut.because: The team's automation code is competent. The problem is what they were asked to automate, and when.

locations.name: The Quotes team room
locations.summary: Desks, a whiteboard and last night's red build on every screen.
locations.intro: Monday morning. The nightly build failed again, and the team room is quiet in the way rooms get when nobody wants to say it out loud.

hotspots.label: Open feature file
hotspots.note: The Quotes repo is open on a feature file full of clicks, waits and CSS selectors.

hotspots.label: Test-data sheet
hotspots.note: The sheet every scenario uses to log in, with a warning scrawled in red.

hotspots.label: Printed ticket
hotspots.note: A CI hardware request is taped to the cabinet.

hotspots.label: Sticky note
hotspots.note: "Step repo mirror code = number of scenarios in the suite." Useful later.

hotspots.label: Team chat
hotspots.note: "#quotes-ci: nightly run FAILED. 37 failed, 41 passed on retry." Nobody has reacted.

hotspots.label: Plant
hotspots.note: Plastic. Nobody had time to water a real one.

locations.name: The adoption memo
locations.summary: The plan that introduced Cucumber 18 months ago.
locations.prompt: Highlight the line that explains how scenarios get written.

lines.text: Goal: replace manual regression testing with automated Cucumber tests.
lines.note: The goal is test automation; collaboration isn't mentioned.

lines.text: QA will convert existing manual test cases into feature files after each release. Developers and product are not expected to change how they work.
Scenarios will be automated through the web UI to match how testers test today.
lines.note: So every scenario drives the browser.

lines.text: Success measure: number of automated scenarios.
lines.note: Counting scenarios rewards quantity, not clarity.

locations.name: Pipeline config
locations.summary: The nightly CI job for the Quotes suite.

lines.note: Nightly only: developers get feedback the next morning at best.
Reports are generated. Nobody outside QA opens them.
Part of the same problem: failures are rerun until they pass.

locations.name: Last night's run report
locations.summary: The numbers from the most recent nightly run.

lines.text: Total: 600 scenarios, 3 h 04 min, 37 failed, 41 passed only on retry.
Time in browser-driven steps: 2 h 46 min (90%).
Slowest feature: premium_by_age_and_region.feature, 1 Scenario Outline, 120 Examples rows, 22 min.
CI node CPU: average 9%, one core busy.
Longest scenario: "Full quote-to-payment journey", 46 steps, 7 min.
lines.note: A long journey testing many behaviours: one failure hides everything after it.

locations.name: Commit history
locations.summary: When code and feature files arrived, story by story.
locations.rule: In BDD, a story's examples are agreed before or while its code is written.

mismatches.note: Six weeks after the code, added by QA alone.
The same pattern: Gherkin arrives long after the behaviour is built.
Again. The Claims rows show the opposite order.

locations.okNote: This story's examples were written before the code, together.

locations.name: How a Quotes story moves
locations.summary: Rebuild the life of a story, from ticket to nightly run.
locations.prompt: Put the steps in the order they really happen in the Quotes team.

events.text: The product owner writes the story ticket.
Developers build it from the ticket.
The story is released to production.
QA converts the manual test case into a feature file.
QA automates the scenario through the browser.
The scenario joins the nightly run.

locations.solvedNote: Nowhere in this flow do product, development and testing sit down to agree examples before building. The Gherkin arrives weeks after the code has shipped.

locations.name: Two suites, one company
locations.summary: The Quotes suite beside the Claims team's.
locations.prompt: Compare the two suites row by row. Where do they really differ?

spots.note: Same tool, same language, same servers: none of those can explain the gap.
Quotes describes the screen; Claims describes the business.
Claims agrees its examples before building; Quotes records them afterwards.
Claims' scenarios are independent, so they can run in parallel.

locations.name: Step-definition repo
locations.summary: A read-only mirror of the Quotes step definitions.
locations.lockedNote: Look around the team room first.
locations.prompt: The mirror asks for a three-digit project code. Someone left a note about it in the team room.
hints: The sticky note said the code is a count.
It's the number of scenarios in the Quotes suite, from the briefing.
locations.openText: The mirror opens on QuoteSteps.java. The first lines declare the browser and the current policy as static fields, shared by every step class.

locations.name: Sam's trial run
locations.summary: Try the same Gherkin automated in different ways.
locations.intro: Sam rewrote a slice of Quotes scenarios declaratively and offers to run them in different set-ups.
locations.prompt: Choose how the steps are automated and how test data is handled, then estimate the nightly run.

outcomes.text: Today's set-up: every step drives the browser and everything runs one at a time.
API steps are much faster, but shared data still forces a one-at-a-time run.
Independent data lets 8 workers run in parallel, but every step still drives a browser.
Same tool, rewritten scenarios: below the UI, each with its own data, in parallel.

locations.name: Interview: Iris
locations.summary: The product owner who stopped reading the scenarios.
locations.opening: "I wanted to read them. I really did. I gave up about a year ago."

questions.ask: Why did you stop reading the feature files?
questions.answer: "They're all clicks, selectors and waits. I can't tell which business rule any of them checks."

questions.ask: Were you ever asked about examples before a story was built?
questions.answer: "Never. I write the ticket, developers build it, and QA writes scenarios after it ships. That's what the plan said."

questions.ask: The Claims product owner helps write their scenarios. Would you?
questions.answer: "If they read like the Claims ones, gladly. Theirs read like our rule book."

locations.name: Interview: Lena
locations.summary: The platform engineer who runs the CI pool.
locations.opening: "The Quotes nightly job is my least favourite thing on the whole platform."

questions.ask: How hard do the CI servers work during the run?
questions.answer: "Not hard at all, oddly. The node sits around 9% CPU for three hours, one core busy."

questions.ask: What would fix the run time?
questions.answer: "Honestly? Give me 64-core machines and this would fly."
questions.note: More cores can't help a suite that runs one scenario at a time with parallel switched off; the servers already sit idle.

questions.ask: Why is parallel execution switched off?
questions.answer: "It used to be on. Scenarios kept breaking each other: same login, same data. So we turned it off and added two retries. That stopped most of the noise."

locations.name: Interview: Dana
locations.summary: The QA lead whose team wrote the scenarios.
locations.opening: "My team did exactly what we were asked to do. Nobody else had time."

questions.ask: How strong is your team at automation?
questions.answer: "Strong. Two are certified in browser automation, they built a clean page-object framework, and code reviews rate their Java highly."

questions.ask: Who decides what the scenarios say?
questions.answer: "We do, from the old manual test cases, after each release. Product and dev never asked to be involved."

questions.ask: Why do the step classes share state through static fields?
questions.answer: "Steps had to pass the browser and the policy along, and static was the quickest way. Then parallel runs started breaking, so parallel got switched off."

board.heading: The case board
board.intro: Pin each clue, then string it to the theories it fits or contradicts. A contradiction rules a theory out; fitting is not proof.

accusation.intro: Choose the explanation every piece of evidence converges on, and say how sure you are.

epilogue.heading: Epilogue
epilogue.concept: BDD is a practice, not a tool
paragraphs: Lumen didn't have a Cucumber problem. It had adopted the tool without the practice. BDD starts with a conversation before code: product, development and testing agree concrete examples of behaviour (discovery, often with Example Mapping), write them down in Gherkin (formulation), and only then automate them. Quotes skipped straight to automation, weeks after release, using old test cases as the source.

Everything else followed. Scenarios written by testers from manual scripts became imperative click sequences nobody else could read. They shared logins and static state, so parallel runs broke and were switched off; retries papered over the flakiness; exhaustive Outlines and long journeys bloated the run. The Claims team, with the same tool, language and servers, shows what happens when the practice comes first.

The fix is not a new tool. It's discovery sessions before building, declarative scenarios in business language, a per-scenario context injected with PicoContainer instead of statics, independent test data, automation below the UI wherever possible, flakiness fixed at its source, and tags such as @smoke for a fast check on every commit.
takeaways: Agree examples before code; Gherkin written after release is just slow regression testing.
Write declarative steps that describe behaviour; keep clicks and selectors in the step definitions.
Keep scenarios independent: no static fields, shared accounts or run-order dependencies.
Automate below the UI where you can; most speed comes from there.
Fix flaky scenarios at the source instead of hiding them behind retries.
When the same tool works for another team, look at the practice, not the tool.
